title: A simple pattern
hookLine: many Protestant churches teach adoration, confession, thanksgiving, supplication as a shape for prayer

cards: Blank-page panic. You sit down to write a birthday card, a toast, a hard email, and nothing comes. Then someone says: just do three things.
Say what you love about them, tell one story, raise your glass. Suddenly it's easy. A shape helps.

Prayer goes the same way. Eyes close, and the mind goes blank, or straight to a shopping list: help me, fix that. So many Protestant churches, especially evangelical ones, teach a four-letter shape to hang a prayer on.
It spells a book of the Bible you've just spent weeks in. A, C, T, S.

teach.b: A is for adoration. Before asking anything, you start with who God is, the way the Psalms do: "O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker." Not thanks yet; just wonder at who he is.
C is for confession: being honest about where you've gone wrong. The first letter of John puts it simply: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins."
Catholics and Orthodox also have confession as a sacrament with a priest; many Protestants confess directly to God, alone or together in a service.
T is for thanksgiving: naming what you're grateful for, specifically.
S is for supplication, an old word for asking, humbly, for yourself and for others.

Paul packs almost the whole shape into one line to the church in Philippi: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God."
Be careful for nothing means don't be anxious about anything. Notice the order: asking comes last.
By then you've remembered who you're talking to, been honest, and said thank you, and the asking often comes out different.
Nobody knows exactly who first put these four letters together; it's a modern teaching tool, not a verse. But the shape is old.
The Lord's Prayer says hallowed be thy name before it gets to daily bread, and many written liturgies follow a similar path. ACTS just carries it in your pocket.

how: Many Protestant, especially evangelical, churches teach ACTS (adoration, confession, thanksgiving, supplication) as a pattern for personal and group prayer. Churches with set liturgies follow a similar movement of praise, confession, thanks and intercession in their services.

o: a list of good deeds to do every single day
a creed said aloud in Protestant services
a four-part shape for prayer, with asking last

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: honesty about where you went wrong
asking, humbly, for yourself and others

s: the ACTS pattern is written in the Bible
it's a modern teaching tool. the shape is old, but the four letters aren't a verse.
asking comes last, after adoration, confession and thanks.
Paul puts prayer, supplication and thanksgiving in one line to the Philippians
in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.

games.q: you sit down to pray and your mind goes straight to a list of things you need. using the ACTS shape, where do you start?
games.why: adoration comes first: O come, let us worship and bow down. by the time you reach supplication, the asking often comes out different.

practice: If you pray, go through the four letters slowly, one sentence each: one thing about God that fills you with wonder, one honest thing you got wrong, one specific thing from today, one thing you or someone else needs.

Leave a little silence between each. If you don't pray, try the shape anyway: something that fills you with wonder, something you'd do differently, something you're grateful for, something you hope for.

wordCard.voice: ACTS. Adoration, confession, thanksgiving, supplication. This week: take and read, Francis, Teresa, Joan, the story you're in, prayer, and a shape.
